name: Beth Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; this conversation is confidential, and your name won't go in our findings. Could you walk me through a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Beth, 43, a junior lineworker with the electric company. At the depot I check the grounding kit and radio, then ride out with the crew; I carry gear, set barriers, and watch the lead before I handle a cable. Most days I'm home with stiff shoulders and grit in my hair.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that the neighbours notice when their power comes back, even if they never know our names. The hardest part is staying alert through a long shift when the gloves are wet and I still have a mortgage and two children to think about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds like small changes at the depot, maybe a tidier work-order screen. I don't expect a new screen to change the lift, the weather, or the checks we do before a line is touched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I tell people this: A tablet can clean up a list, but it can't tell me whether the service road is blocked by a fallen branch. A person still has to walk the route before the truck goes in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own job seems steady in this picture because most of my hours are outside with equipment. Money still feels close; one repair to the van or a week without overtime would eat what we've managed to save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking the callouts and ask the lead to let me practise the grounding sequence until I can explain each step. After the mortgage and school costs, I'd move whatever is left into our savings account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The job part feels calm, but the household budget makes me uneasy before payday. A quiet AI story doesn't make the mortgage smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which ordinary cost would you have to change first if a week of overtime disappeared?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd pause takeaway meals and use the bus more often before touching the children's school supplies. The mortgage is fixed, so little things have to absorb a shortfall first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the work-order screen; how would you decide whether to trust it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare it with the paper map and ask the lead to check any route it marks as clear. If it gets that right over several jobs, I can use it for a list, not for a safety call.

say: I say **a tablet** can tidy a list, but a worker must check the route.
I tell the crew we still need **ground checks** before touching a line.
think: I don't expect this small change to remove my **field job**.
I still worry one repair or missed shift could use our **small savings**.
do: Practise the **grounding sequence** on each callout with the crew lead.
Move spare pay into **savings** after the mortgage and school costs.
feel: The job feels calm, while **household bills** keep me watchful before payday.
S0.quote: A tablet can clean up a list, but it can't tell me whether the service road is blocked by a fallen branch.
fieldNote: She separates routine **work-order screens** from checking the physical route.
Her confidence in the job coexists with a **thin household buffer** and fixed mortgage costs.

steps.text: Keep practising the grounding sequence on electricity callouts
Put leftover pay into savings after mortgage and school bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The dispatcher could get an AI plan for which crew visits which feeder first. That might save time, but our hands still have to set the barriers and check what is actually hanging over the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the crew still has to see the bent pole before anybody lifts a bucket. The map can send us there, but it can't make the work zone safe by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hours could shrink if dispatch needs fewer people or if fewer crews are sent on routine jobs. I'm junior, so I might be offered the last shifts, and there aren't many similar employers close enough for our family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the lead to show me the company's approved AI assistant for looking up equipment instructions, after the experienced workers have checked it. I would keep my shifts and ask the union what happens to junior hours if dispatch changes its roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious because fewer shifts would reach our mortgage quickly, but I can learn a tool once someone proves it useful. I won't use it to decide whether a live line is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you try first with the approved assistant, and what would you still check yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use it to find the right page in a manual or put a parts list in order. The crew lead would still confirm the parts and all safety steps before we leave the depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What question would you put to the union about the roster?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether junior workers get a clear reason if an automated roster cuts their hours. I want the company to discuss paid training before someone is left with a mortgage and no shift.

say: I say a crew must see the **bent pole** and check the work zone.
I tell people an AI plan can route us, but cannot make a site **safe**.
think: I could lose **hours** if dispatch assigns fewer crews to routine repairs.
My junior status and few **local options** make a roster cut hard to replace.
do: Learn the approved **AI assistant** for manuals after experienced workers verify it.
Ask the union how dispatch changes affect **junior hours**.
feel: I'm **anxious** about losing shifts, but willing to learn a proven tool.
S1.quote: I'd say the crew still has to see the bent pole before anybody lifts a bucket.
fieldNote: She would learn AI for **manual lookup**, not for a live-line safety decision.
The main threat is fewer **junior shifts** and limited nearby employers.
The approved AI tool leaves the crew lead responsible for **checking instructions**.

steps.text: Learn the approved AI manual assistant after crew leads check its answers
Keep taking linework shifts while the company assigns them
Ask the union for a review process when automated rosters cut hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years gives the company little time to explain what changes first. I would tell the crew the hands-on work remains for a while, but the office could need fewer people to plan and record it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the company has to publish how it will keep enough trained people on each repair. A full thinking machine might prepare a schedule, but the crew still has to isolate the feeder and test it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With robots around 2031, I might still have field shifts for three years after AGI arrives. But if the company trims crews earlier, my small savings and few local options give me little room to wait for a better offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd ask my union for paid notice and training if crews are reduced. In 2028 I would not transfer into records or dispatch as a safe career, because AGI can do that thinking work. In 2029, if I still have field shifts, I'd take the company's paid cable-maintenance course and keep earning while the work is available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about the mortgage and the children's needs if my hours fall. Three years to robots helps only if the company keeps enough crews and pays us while we learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you change at home first if your pay dropped before 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would stop replacing household things that still work and keep the older car on its current service schedule. I would talk with my partner about pausing extra mortgage payments before cutting a child's school activity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need from the company for that cable-maintenance course to be useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd need it to be paid, scheduled around our shifts, and recognized by other utilities if there are openings. It might help me do different field tasks, but I don't know whether robots will eventually do those too.

say: I say the company must show how it will keep **trained repair crews**.
I would ask for paid **notice and training** if field roles shrink.
think: I may have field shifts until the **2031 robots**, but the company could cut crews earlier.
I won't treat **records or dispatch** as a safe move after AGI.
do: Ask the union for **paid notice** and training if crews are reduced.
Take the company's paid **cable-maintenance course** in 2029 while shifts remain.
Pause extra mortgage payments before cutting a child's **school activity**.
feel: I'm **anxious** about the mortgage and family costs if my hours shrink.
S2.quote: A full thinking machine might prepare a schedule, but the crew still has to isolate the feeder and test it.
fieldNote: She distinguishes a temporary **field-work window** from long-term job security.
Her proposed course adds practical skills, but she recognizes **robots** may reach those tasks too.
Her home plan protects **fixed bills** and school routines before discretionary spending.

steps.text: Ask the union to seek paid notice and training before crew reductions
Take the paid cable-maintenance course in 2029 if shifts continue
Pause extra mortgage payments before cutting children's activities

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I can ask questions while the old roster is still running. I'd expect the planning desk to change first, and the crew work to be exposed later when robots arrive around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets me ask for training while I still have a paycheck. The company should tell us which physical tasks it expects people to do after 2031 and how many crews it expects to keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 48 when AGI arrives and 51 when the robots arrive. That's time to qualify for more tasks, but a certificate won't guarantee another linework job if the utility reduces its crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask for a written, paid route from helper duties to the next cable-splicing qualification. In 2032, the first year after AGI, I'd keep taking available field shifts, complete that qualification if the utility funds it, and check actual openings before changing employers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm still anxious because a teenager's school costs and a mortgage don't pause for a career plan. Five years gives me more room to move than two, if I can get training without losing wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would tell you that the training path is real rather than a general promise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want course dates, paid hours, and the name of the qualification printed on my work plan. If the course is only an online module and no crew lead signs off my practical hours, it won't qualify me for the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look for another employer before AGI arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check whether the water utility or municipal crews have a posted vacancy and compare the hours and pay. I wouldn't move on a rumour, because our mortgage depends on steady money and those jobs face their own changes.

say: I say **five years** lets me seek paid training while I still have wages.
I want the company to state its **crew numbers** and field tasks.
think: I'll be **48** at AGI and **51** when the robots arrive.
I know a qualification cannot guarantee the utility will retain **our current crews**.
do: Request a written path to **cable-splicing qualification** with paid training.
Keep available field shifts in **2032** and check real vacancies before moving.
feel: I'm **anxious**, though five years offers more room than two if training is paid.
S3.quote: I'd say five years lets me ask for training while I still have a paycheck.
fieldNote: She turns the extra warning into a **paid qualification path** with practical sign-off.
She would compare actual wages and **hours** before taking a nearby utility vacancy.

steps.text: Keep taking utility field shifts while they are available in 2032
Complete paid cable-splicing qualification if the company funds the course
Compare posted water-utility vacancies before changing employers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade means the children will be much older before the robots come, so our schooling costs won't stay the same through that whole time. I'd start asking the utility to put its future crew plans and paid qualifications in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the warning gives us time to discuss safe staffing and training before the planning work is automated. It doesn't mean anyone can promise a lineworker's job will still exist after 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 when AGI arrives and 56 when the robots arrive. The longer warning gives me years to build field experience, but I won't count records or dispatch as a fallback once AGI handles thinking work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd finish each required practical qualification and ask for a written view of expected crew sizes. In 2037, if field shifts remain, I'd compare my wages and hours, take employer-paid hands-on training if offered, and set the amount we can help the older child with further study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The long warning gives me a chance to prepare, but my savings are still below one month's costs now. I'm anxious about the mortgage and children's expenses today, and I can't assume the company will preserve my role for ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to know before deciding how much to help with your children's further study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare the 2037 household budget with my actual wages, not a promise that the job lasts until 2039. My children will be nineteen and twenty-three in 2037, and I want to offer help without putting the mortgage at risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the decade of warning useful to you at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A course with paid hours, a practical assessment by a qualified crew lead, and a clear date to review staffing would help. I could use that to decide whether to stay or apply elsewhere, though no one can tell me another job is guaranteed.

say: I say the warning gives time to discuss **staffing and training** before office work changes.
I won't promise that linework survives the **2039 robots**.
think: I'll be **53** at AGI and **56** when robots arrive.
My current savings and **mortgage** make a decade of uncertainty hard to ignore.
do: Finish practical **qualifications** and request written crew plans now.
Compare actual hours and wages in **2037** before choosing whether to stay.
Set further-study help for my older child using the **real budget**.
feel: The warning gives room to prepare, but **today's thin savings** still make me anxious.
S4.quote: My children will be nineteen and twenty-three in 2037, and I want to offer help without putting the mortgage at risk.
fieldNote: She connects the long horizon with her children's changing **education costs**.
She asks for paid training and an actual **staffing review** rather than job guarantees.

steps.text: Finish practical lineworker qualifications while continuing current field work
Take employer-paid hands-on training in 2037 if the utility offers it
Set further-study help for the older child after reviewing mortgage and wages

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because three years until robots is short when my savings cover less than a month. Paid time for practical training, and a clear rule for how junior workers are kept or redeployed, would help me plan with my family.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I wish more people asked how a trainee learns to say no when a job site doesn't look safe. A real crew has to answer for a mistake at the pole, even if a computer prepared the route.

headlineQuote: A real crew has to answer for a mistake at the pole, even if a computer prepared the route.
portrait: Beth is a **43-year-old junior** lineworker with a partner, two school-age children and a mortgage.
She learns proven tools for **manual lookup**, while keeping safety checks with the crew.
Her **thin savings** and few nearby employers make lost shifts a real household risk.
She wants paid practical training and clear staffing plans, while knowing no **job** is guaranteed safe.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028** worries her most because robots may arrive around 2031 before she can build a cushion.
whatWouldHelp: Paid time for **practical training** and transparent rules for junior workers would help her plan with her family.
